items: Agnes Callamard warns that US sanctions against the ICC could jeopardize Rodrigo Duterte's upcoming trial for crimes against humanity related to his war on drugs.
Japan has reaffirmed its support for the ICC by committing to early financial contributions, which could help mitigate the impact of US sanctions on the court's operations.

There is an unexpected intersection between United States President Donald Trump and former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Former United Nations rapporteur and current Amnesty International secretary general Agnes Callamard warned that Trump’s continued threats against the International Criminal Court (ICC) could jeopardize Duterte’s crimes against humanity case at The Hague, Netherlands.

Duterte’s trial begins on November 30 — he is the first Filipino and Asian head of state to face trial over the same case. The charge stemmed from his war on drugs and the killings attributed to the Davao Death Squad.

“The trial of ex-president Duterte is due to start on 30 November. It could take one year or probably more until judgment. If no action is taken to protect the ICC against the US sanctions, the trial may never proceed,” Callamard told Rappler.
Groups have warned that US sanctions against the ICC could affect its operations, including its investigations.

“The US sanctions against the ICC and those who support its work put justice at risk in situations across the court’s docket, from the Philippines, to Sudan, to Palestine. Governments should take every available measure to counter the effects of the US sanctions and stand with the court and those relying on it to obtain justice,” Human Rights Watch senior counsel Maria Elena Vignoli told Rappler.
Former ICC judge and current drug war Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan said in an interview that US sanctions are serious threats and a cause of concern.

However, Pangalangan explained that even in the event that the likes of Trump are successful in tearing down the international tribunal, Duterte’s trial will still continue. This is because the court has already acquired jurisdiction over the case, he said.

“You see, if you look at the other courts which have wound up their operations, if a case has begun, in this case, it’s not just a preliminary examination or investigation. It is now the actual trial. In all those other cases, once the trial has begun, it continues,” the former ICC judge told Rappler.

“So even in the worst scenario that they do succeed to dismantle the court, that jurisdiction, once acquired, will have to be carried out. So that means that the case…the trial will go on until the end. At least, that is my hope,” he added.

blocks.text: An important factor in ensuring the ICC’s survival is the support of other powerful countries.
While Callamard said some nations, including Canada and the United Kingdom, refuse to protect the court, she is still urging states to stand up for the court.

On November 24, Japan proved itself to be a reliable ally of the court. During her meeting with ICC president Tomoko Akane, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her country will pay its ICC contribution for 2027 before the year ends.

Japan is the ICC’s largest financial contributor, accounting for at least 15% of the court’s budget. It is followed by Germany, France, Britain, Italy, South Korea, and Canada. The early contribution would allow the ICC to have access to funding before US sanctions take effect in April 2027.
Japan’s move would encourage other major contributors to make early payments, “creating a meaningful cash buffer before sanctions bite,” said analysts cited by Reuters.

“It is also my hope that the court will remain steadfast for as long as it has the support of the EU and especially in Asia — of Japan and Korea. And it looks like that solid base of support will remain,” Pangalangan said. – with a report from Reuters/Rappler.com
